title: What Advanced asks of you
lead: What the Court expects of an Advanced Sommelier, how the course and the three exam sections work, how the theory exam is built, and a study system that covers it all.

intro.title: THE ADVANCED PATH
intro.text: Advanced is two separate steps: a course, then an exam in three sections. All three sections must be passed in the same calendar year.

lines.label: What it is
lines.text: The Court's own list of what an Advanced Sommelier can do: deep theory, top-level formal service, deductive tasting and running a whole beverage program.

lines.label: Who holds it
lines.text: Floor and head sommeliers, beverage directors of a single restaurant or hotel, and people in winery hospitality, retail, importing and distribution.

know: The skill set has four parts: theory, formal service, deductive tasting and beverage program management.
Service at Advanced covers still and sparkling wine, decanting, beer, after-dinner drinks and by-the-glass pours.
Service also covers classic cocktails and spirits, food and wine pairing, and benchmark producers and vintages.
Program management means the list, cellar design, purchasing, inventory, staff training and cost control with spreadsheets.
Training includes mentoring staff toward the Court's Introductory and Certified levels.

lines.text: 60 minutes, about 115 questions, on a computer at a Pearson VUE center. No calculator: costing is tested in the Practical.

lines.label: Scoring
lines.text: Wrong answers cost nothing, so answer everything. Master Sommeliers hand-grade, so exact spelling and accents aren't required.

know: Question types include multiple choice, short answer, matching, maps, labels and ordering lists.

No essays, no 'list them all' questions and no opinion questions.
Questions give US and metric units; answer in either.

lines.label: Breadth and depth
lines.text: The Court's topic list gives breadth: every region and drink. Its Areas of Study give depth: one checklist you run on each of them.

lines.label: Two questions
lines.text: For every subject ask: why does it taste the way it does, and what do I need to know to serve it at the table?

know: Areas of Study for wine: place, climate, grapes, vineyard, winery, soils, styles, law, vintages, terms, producers, history and service.
Vintage study is for major age-worthy regions: the last 15 years, how good each was and why.
Research about five iconic producers per region, at every level of quality and price.
Weight your time: Tuscany and Piedmont deserve more hours than Basilicata or Molise.
The Court's own Hospitality & Service standards are the only ones accepted on its exams.

facts.fact: Expected skill set: in-depth theoretical knowledge of major beverage alcohol; world-class formal service (still, sparkling, red wine decanting, beer, after-dinner and glass pour service; global food and wine pairing salesmanship; classic cocktail production and spirits service; benchmark producers and vintages; hospitality and salesmanship); deductive tasting for a broad spectrum of classic reds and whites; complete beverage program management (list content, design and marketing; cellar design, purchasing and inventory; staff training including mentorship toward Introductory or Certified; financial management with cost controls and spreadsheets).

Potential roles: Floor Sommelier, Head Sommelier, Beverage Director of a single-unit restaurant or hotel; Winery Hospitality Management, Retail Manager/Owner, Distributor and/or Importer Educator or Senior Salesperson.
The Advanced course and exam are held independently; students must attend the course before applying for the exam.
The Advanced Sommelier Course is a three-day program of classroom lectures giving a template for upper-level exam study, plus small breakout tasting sessions with individualized feedback.
The Court recommends waiting at least one calendar year after passing the Certified exam before the Advanced course.

Course eligibility: passed Certified; restaurant service/sales experience; current employment in restaurant, hospitality or beverage industry (retail, distribution, winery, education); not attended the three-day course before.

The SKA is required for all course applicants: about 55 minutes, in person at a Pearson or Pearson-approved testing center, randomized questions across Theory, Tasting and Practical (Hospitality & Service and Business of the Sommelier). Exam applicants do not take the SKA.
Applicants can apply for the course or the exam, not both. RALIANCE online training is a prerequisite for the course and exam.
The exam has three sections: Theory (written), Tasting (verbal), Practical (Hospitality and Service; Business of the Sommelier).

Theory is taken first at a Pearson VUE testing center; passing it brings an invitation to the Practical and Tasting later in the year. Failing Theory means waiting until the next calendar year. All three must be passed in one calendar year; passing Theory but not Practical and/or Tasting means starting again with Theory the next year.
Passing requirement: a minimum of 60% on each section within one calendar year.
Forced wait: a first Practical below 40%, or a second consecutive year's Practical below 50%. No required minimum on any Tasting attempt.
Exam eligibility includes at least three years in a restaurant service or sales job, having attended the three-day course, and current employment in the restaurant, hospitality or beverage industry.

Business of the Sommelier is the first portion of the Practical: a timed 50-minute exam with tasting and evaluating beverages, costing wine, cocktails and flights, reading and evaluating inventory sheets, and correcting a beverage list. A calculator is provided; no negative points.

Hospitality & Service follows immediately: about 15-20 minutes of preparation with the situation, guest notes, menus, wine list and beverage list; two tables per panel with a maître d' who cannot answer content questions; besides cocktails, beverages are poured tableside.
Tasting exam: six wines, 25 minutes, three to four Master Sommelier adjudicators; time calls at halfway, five minutes and one minute.

Theory exam: 60-minute timed exam with approximately 115 questions. Types: multiple choice, short answer, matching, map identification, label identification, ordering lists (lowest to highest, geography, age, aging, process steps), vintage knowledge, producer knowledge, applying tasting and service knowledge. US and metric units both given; either accepted.
Not asked: essays, multiple-answer 'list all' questions, opinion questions, and Business of the Sommelier costing/math questions (no calculator needed at Theory).

Five minutes to read and accept the NDA, not counted against exam time; the timer starts at the first question. Flag questions for review; plan time to return to them. No score deductions: answer every question. Spelling, grammar and accents not required; Master Sommeliers hand-grade.
Theory exam timeline: arrive 15 minutes early; 5 minutes NDA; 60 minutes exam; 5-minute anonymous exit survey. No personal items in the testing room.
At least 60% to pass Theory; results, scores and feedback within four weeks, including the overall percentage and performance in key areas.
Theory answers on sweetness, acidity, alcohol, body and tannin use Deductive Tasting Method terminology; volumes, distances and aging use the units given in the question.

The example feedback report describes four question types: simple short answer; extrapolation simple short answer (complex terms); complex structure with a qualifier; logical reasoning (short explanation of a concept).
Feedback bands: 75% and up Excellent; 60-74% Strong; 50-59% Fair; 49% and under Developing.

Topics fall into Cause & Effect (geography, grape growing, law, vintage climate, style and type, winemaking) and Tableside (history and lore, label terms, producer, vintage price and reputation), with overlap.

Systematic approach to study = General Theory Topics (breadth) + Areas of Study (depth). Holistic approach: taste what you study; don't wait to pass Theory before studying Tasting, Service and Business. Two questions for every subject: why does it taste the way it does, and what do I need to know to serve it tableside.

Make a flexible timeline; prioritize buckets of major and minor regions (more time on Tuscany and Piedmont than Basilicata or Molise); go back to the basics, since many hard-looking questions draw on basic knowledge.
Study ideas include flashcards, tracing maps, study groups, and teaching staff or colleagues how to explain information to a guest.

Areas of Study for wine: location and geography, climate, grape varieties, grape growing, winemaking, soils, wine styles, wine law, vintage knowledge (major age-worthy regions, last 15 years), terminology, major producers (five most iconic per region at all ranges of quality and price), history and lore, and hospitality, service and business.
The Hospitality & Service standards published by CMS-A are the only accepted service standards for any CMS-A examination.

unverified: Exam experience window: the Court's web page says three years within the last seven; the Theory Exam guide PDF says three years within nine (extended from seven due to COVID-19). The lesson says only 'three years' and points to the Court's page.
Course experience: the web page reads 'at least two (2) of restaurant experience' within seven years; the unit is missing (likely years). The lesson doesn't state a number.
Third-attempt forced wait: the web page names a third consecutive Practical below 55%; the Theory guide PDF says a third consecutive Theory or Practical below 55%. Left out of the lesson.
The Theory guide says the course must be attended before October of the application year; the web page says only that the course must be attended before applying. Left out.
The skill set is worded slightly differently in the Skill Set PDF and the Theory guide (the guide adds assessing drinks for style, quality and thematic fit). The lesson uses wording both share.
The feedback score bands come from the Court's example report; the Court may change them.
